stories.body:
Family run private businesses helped power China’s economic miracle, but the next generation is finding it difficult to carry on the work of their parents

G rowing up, Ayu would watch his parents put together hand made leather shoes on the ground floor of their three storey home in the Chinese city of Wenzhou. Their relatives in Europe would send photographs of designer products from Italy for the workers to base their designs on, and in the decades that followed, the tiny family-run workshop transformed into a 700 person factory.

“The factory and the home were the same place. I watched them make shoes by hand, piece by piece, using small machines,” Ayu recalls of watching his parents work in the 1980’s.

By the mid eighties, Chinese economists had a name for this type of bottom up economic growth story: the Wenzhou model. It was a system that saw small companies secure finances through family connections and operate underground factories to produce cheap goods that would end up on the busy streets of China and beyond.

But now many of the family-run manufacturing businesses that helped to fuel China’s economic success are facing a succession crisis, with the children of factory owners unable or unwilling to take them over.

Ayu – who today runs an online e-commerce platform – says it’s not that his generation doesn’t want to take them over, but that the market is much more competitive than when their parents started, and the crucial institutional knowledge and commercial relationships that powered their success will be impossible to pass on.

Personal relationships, experience and instincts are difficult to hand over to the next generation, says Hanqing Fang, an associate professor at Missouri University of Science and Technology.

“Shares can be passed to a son or daughter overnight,” Fang says. “But the heir is being asked to take over something that looks like a company on paper but, in practice, is closer to the founder’s personal belongings.”

“The network is very difficult to inherit,” Ayu says. “You have to build it yourself. In the end, some people inherit an empty shell. On paper they’re the boss, but the people underneath them have already begun to leave.

“We inherited the wealth, but we couldn’t inherit the industry.”

‘I’m not ready yet, because it’s not easy’

According to HSBC Life research, two-thirds of wealthy Chinese people have no legacy plan. In a study led by the University of Ningbo, just 10 out of 114 private companies surveyed said they were being managed by the families’ second generation.

Many of China’s second generation business owners speak of a profound anxiety about taking over the family firm.

“I really don’t want to take over because there are so many interpersonal relationships and financial connections that I’d have to handle and learn about,” says Wu, a graduate who works in marketing in Hong Kong.

His family own a snack processing factory in the Chinese city of Shanwei, as well as dozens of stores in Shenzhen and Hong Kong. But he is reluctant to join the family business.

“Most young people dream of getting rich overnight, but I know there’s no such thing. When inheriting a fortune, you also have to consider all the complicated paperwork and whether you really have the ability to handle those responsibilities,” Wu says.

According to official estimates, China’s private sector accounts for more than half of the country’s tax revenue and 60% of its GDP . Economists say unsuccessful handovers can lead to firms losing value or even closing.

Because family-run companies represent such a large percentage of China’s private sector, if they fail in their thousands it could threaten the country’s future growth.

“The risk is not that these family firms simply disappear. It is that the capabilities embedded in the founder – including the knowhow, the supplier networks and the relationships – are lost in the handover,” Fang says.

For Wu, the idea of one day taking control of the family business is not completely out of the question, but he concedes he still has a lot to learn.

“I’d say that one day my parents’ company will be mine. But I’m not ready yet, because it’s not easy,” Wu says.

“If I could just have the money without any responsibilities, I’d take it without hesitation. But the thing is, it’s not that simple.”

stories.title: RFK Jr. unveils sweeping federal initiative to find evidence of vaccine injuries
stories.summary: "[T]he Trump-RFK Jr anti-vax agenda keeps getting more corrupt and dangerous."
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
“[T]he Trump-RFK Jr anti-vax agenda keeps getting more corrupt and dangerous.”

Under anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the federal health department is undertaking an agency-wide effort to focus on injuries claimed to be related to vaccines.

In a press announcement Thursday , the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) laid out four aspects of the large-scale initiative. The first is a new clinic at the National Institutes of Health that is “dedicated to studying and caring for patients experiencing health problems following vaccination.” Despite only being announced today, the clinic actually opened October 5, and Kennedy secretly attended its ribbon-cutting ceremony alongside other high-level Trump administration officials. It’s unclear why his visit and the clinic’s opening were not disclosed by the Trump administration, but they were reported by Bloomberg Law at the time.

Another aspect of the initiative is a proposal to reimburse doctors for reporting possible injuries from vaccines to a federal system called VAERS, or the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System. VAERS, which is run by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, is a common focus of anti-vaccine advocates , who incessantly misuse it . The system is meant to be an indiscriminate dragnet of any potential safety concerns linked to vaccines, providing a sensitive early warning monitoring system. Anyone, including members of the public, can submit an unvetted report.

The CDC continuously monitors and assesses those reports, finding that the vast majority are not actually related to vaccinations. Still, anti-vaccine advocates—particularly those involved in litigation seeking money for alleged vaccine injuries—often point to the trove of unsubstantiated reports on VAERS as evidence that vaccines are dangerous.

“Dangerous”

HHS said the proposal to reimburse doctors for filing VAERS reports will “reduce barriers to physician reporting and encourage health care professionals to document suspected adverse events following vaccination.” The announcement did not make clear how doctors would be paid for VAERS reports, but The New York Times reported that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) may introduce a new billing code to reimburse doctors.

In addition to providing a financial incentive for doctors to submit reports, the HHS is also working to overhaul VAERS to make it “simpler, more accessible, and easier to use.” That includes making the reporting system available on mobile devices—so doctors can report vaccine injuries on the go—and adding more tools for researchers studying vaccine injuries. The CDC has already awarded a nearly $1 million contract to a Virginia-based Christian tech company called SPN Solutions Inc .

Last, Kennedy’s initiative will also require electronic health records to include information about vaccine injuries. This requirement will be carried out through the HHS Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, which oversees federal health information technology standards. HHS said that by adding vaccine injuries to electronic medical records, healthcare providers will have a “more complete picture of a patient’s medical history.”

“We must listen to patients and families who report vaccine injuries—not dismiss or gaslight them,” Kennedy said in a statement. “President Trump and I are building a health system that takes them seriously, follows the evidence, and uses what we learn to make vaccines safer. This is how we earn back trust in our public health institutions.”

Health and medical experts agree that monitoring post-market vaccine safety events is of vital importance—VAERS has been acting as a sensitive early warning system since 1990, and the federal government has several other overlapping safety surveillance systems in place as well. Boosting research on uncommon adverse reactions to vaccines is also welcomed. But experts expect that Kennedy’s goals are not to improve safety or advance research, but instead to continue attacking life-saving vaccines by inflating risks and overemphasizing rare outcomes. He and his anti-vaccine allies have long done this using VAERS in its current form.

“Somehow the Trump-RFK Jr anti-vax agenda keeps getting more corrupt and dangerous,” Brad Woodhouse, president of Protect Our Care, said in a statement Thursday. “Now Secretary Kennedy wants to bribe doctors to claim they see vaccine harm without proof, which is just asking for higher insurance costs and a rash of waste, fraud and abuse.”

stories.title: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring program
stories.summary: An international visa program has for years allowed US tech companies to hire highly skilled workers from abroad.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The White House has often made extreme claims regarding international workers and immigration.

Published 8 October 2026, 19:56 BST

Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program.

Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft alongside other firms of committing fraud through the use of the H1b visa programme and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents.

Vance claimed that Microsoft, one of the most valuable in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants."

Microsoft said most of the H1b visas filed over the last financial year were for existing workers, who are paid the same as local staff.

"No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.

He also made similar accusations about Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.

The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said during the same conference.

Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers.

The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment.

The total number of H1b visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process, is capped , external at 85,000 per year.

A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employs more than 200,000 people worldwide.

Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H1b visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace domestic workers and "undercut" their wages.

The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H1b visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires.

She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H1b visa program are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive.

According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, the median salary , external for an H1b worker at Microsoft is $155,000.

"We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said.

Satya Nadella, Microsoft's longtime CEO, was at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump.

Nadella was also present at other recent White House events, including a luncheon on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping.

Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday.

"Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said.

He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US.

Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US government proposed eliminating , external that grace period altogether.

Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H1b visa program, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more.

None of those companies were included in Vance's Thursday comments.

The program has been aimed at highly skilled or specialized workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades.

The PERM program is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely.

During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Labor certified , external more than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories.

stories.title: UK and Germany will face threats together, says Burnham in Berlin
stories.summary: Ahead of a UK-EU summit next month, Burnham said he was committed to "see if we can bring the UK closer to Europe".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andy Burnham is meeting Chancellor Friedrich Merz on his first official visit to Germany

Published 8 October 2026, 00:01 BST

The UK and Germany will face threats together, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said as he reaffirmed a series of defence and security partnerships.

On his first official European trip, apart from visits to Ukraine, Burnham met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and was greeted with military honours in Berlin.

Speaking to reporters at the German capital's Federal Chancellery, the prime minister said both countries were facing hybrid attacks "on a regular basis" and "it makes sense" to take them on together.

The pair formally ratified the 2025 Kensington Treaty , a partnership committing both countries to tackle hostile activity.

Burnham said the treaty would "improve our security here in Europe" but also help grow the economy and living standards.

"The Kensington Treaty [is] the first treaty between Germany and the UK since the Second World War - it really is a significant moment," he said.

He added that the UK government would now "seek to progress" Germany joining Gcap, the Global Combat Air Programme led by Italy, Japan and the UK to develop a next-generation fighter aircraft.

He outlined partnerships "countering hybrid attacks" and "countering interference in our democratic processes".

He mentioned collaboration on quantum technology and space, adding he was aiming to host the first joint meeting of the UK and German cabinets next year.

The Berlin talks come after intelligence services warned of rising threats, including last month when Germany accused Russia of launching a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

The meeting was held at the Chancellery building in Berlin

Meanwhile, French finance minister Roland Lescure has invited Britain to "come all the way" back to the European Union, in an interview with the BBC's economics editor Faisal Islam.

Ahead of a UK-EU summit next month, Burnham said he was "very committed to securing deeper cooperation" and to "see if we can bring the UK closer to Europe".

He told reporters a closer relationship with Europe was in the interests of growth and tackling irregular migration.

In recent weeks he has mentioned the prospect of eventually rejoining the bloc.

The German leader replied: "From our German side, I can assure you that we will do anything what we can do to bring the UK closer and closer back to Europe, to the European continent, to the European Union."

'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UK Published 17 hours ago

Plans for direct train to Berlin in new UK-Germany treaty Published 17 July 2025

The meeting comes as European leaders have been warning that the threat of hybrid attacks against Europe by Russia has intensified.

Hybrid attacks can include potentially destabilising activity such as cyber attacks, sabotage or misinformation.

Sir Mark Lyall Grant, former UK national security adviser, explained that hybrid warfare "falls somewhere between peace and war - it's in that sort of grey zone, an area where Russia has been extremely active for some time".

He told Radio 4's Today that while Russia had posed a threat to the UK since Vladimir Putin became president in 2001, there had been an "intensification" in response to European support for Ukraine following Russia's invasion.

"We know Russia has been mapping undersea cables in the North Sea; that's something I'm sure Andy Burnham will be talking to Chancellor Merz about because it affects both the UK and Germany," he added.

Last month, a senior Russian diplomat was summoned by the British government over an "egregious and reckless attack" on Leipzig airport, while the EU's foreign affairs chief also summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels.

Burnham was greeted with German military honours

It is a major international freight hub used for providing support to Ukraine. Moscow has denied any involvement in the incident.

Meanwhile, questions have been raised this week about Germany's reliability as an intelligence partner, following the bombshell arrest of a former spy chief on suspicion of espionage .

The talks also come during a period in which Merz's own political future has come under intense scrutiny.

Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, after the former leader was forced out by his own MPs just two years after winning a landslide election victory.

Similarly, Merz has faced persistent rumours he could be replaced by his party due to his poor approval ratings and following setbacks in regional elections .

Although the chancellor appears to have overcome an immediate crisis in his leadership, questions remain over his future.

stories.body:
This post was co-authored by Sheila B. Lalwani , a doctorate student and recent COMPASS Fellow hosted by EFF.

Age verification proposals are often presented as a simple tradeoff: sacrifice a little privacy to better safeguard children online. But that framing overlooks a more fundamental question. What happens to people who cannot verify their age at all? This is particularly a problem when users are required to prove their age with identity documents.

Age-related restrictions are developing quickly around the world. While they differ radically across jurisdictions, in the past year, we’ve witnessed a sharp uptick toward mandatory age assurance for social media access but also for other high-risk digital services.

For example:

In late 2025, Australia became the first country to implement a minimum age requirement for prohibiting children under age 16 from creating or holding social media accounts.

India passed the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act that includes mandatory verifiable parental consent and has undertaken ongoing discussions for social media restriction.

The United Kingdom passed the Online Safety Act requiring age verification across a swath of services hosting content considered harmful to users under 18. More than half the states across the U.S. have enacted age verification laws .

An EU Commission ’s expert report recommends a ban on social media access for users under 13. It also recommends mandatory age verification for platforms to ensure that users are ‘age appropriate.’

The Access Problem

Age verification laws that are predicated on the necessity of users possessing a current passport, driver’s license, credit card, or similar documents proving their identity exclude critical sections of populations. And this problem is global in nature: Millions of people lack government-issued identification or encounter regular challenges to obtaining or updating it.

Roughly 15 million adult U.S. citizens lack a driver’s license, and a further 2.6 million lack any government photo ID ; leaving large groups blocked from online content or services. The UK has a similar predicament: proof-of-age checks are often reliant on passports, driver’s licenses, or other recognized alternatives, which can pose unique challenges to people without these documents.

Much of the advocacy around age verification discusses the privacy harms of age verification. Yet these measures also threaten something more fundamental: equal access to information and the ability to exercise the right to freedom of expression.

Unfortunately, age verification systems foster unequal access to information and provide an asymmetric solution to find essential information, build community, and weigh in on public discourse. As governments and companies increasingly require users to prove their age before accessing online services, these individuals risk being excluded from large parts of the internet altogether.

Effects on Global Majority Countries

Age verification laws reshape who can speak, who can access information, and who gets excluded from the digital public sphere. In other words, age verification is not a neutral safety measure: it presents a structural barrier to disproportionately exclude certain groups—particularly those in the global majority—and alters the architecture of global online expression. Some of these groups are already marginalized offline, and age verification extends that exclusion into digital spaces.

For instance, 850 million people globally do not have ID . Most of these individuals exist in primarily low and middle income countries in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. The World Bank points out that many are members of marginalized groups and more than half of those lacking access to identity documentation also have children whose births have not been registered. Women are particularly vulnerable and are 8% less likely than men to have an ID. Other vulnerable groups, such as adults in low income countries, are less likely to have an ID when they fall below 25 years, as are those with a primary school education or less or those in rural areas.

A policy paper from EDRi points out that age verification laws provide quick tech solutions but overlook longstanding structural challenges and undermine the universality of the internet. The analysis finds that age verification laws have serious human rights implications and ironically harm the very individuals they deem to protect. Moreover, these laws depend on the collection of harmful mass data that human rights organizations, including EFF, is fighting against —and has for decades .

For example:

In Morocco , a push to restrict children’s access would ban under-13s from creating accounts on gaming platforms. This could potentially create challenges for those with IDs that have incomplete information concerning the year of birth. In addition, this push would also impact those who attempt to leave Morocco.

In Egypt , the lack of ID cards has created challenges for minority groups such as the Baha’i.

Stateless individuals would also struggle under age verification laws. The Rohingya , the world’s largest population of stateless people , often lack IDs .

Kuwait’s Bidoon population also lacks proper identification materials. According to Amnesty International , this leads many to rely on standard civil identity cards, which can be restrictive.

Nigeria launched a national program to provide ID cards to its population in 2007. Since then, 64.4 million have registered, but that represents just over 30% of the national population.

The Kafala system, a practice in several countries across the Middle East , also introduces challenges for age verification laws. Under this legal framework, migrant workers’ legal residency and employment status are bound to a specific employer. This potentially leaves stateless persons or migrant workers vulnerable to forced labor and restricted movements.

No ID, No Access

Age verification laws are less about confirming the age of a user and more about creating barriers to online participation that many people cannot reliably scale. The net result is reduced access, more data collection, and an increased chance of unequal or mistaken exclusion from accessing information online.

Nobody doubts the importance of protecting children online. While proponents assert that age verification laws protect minors from harmful material, online harassment, and digital addiction, these laws are not the solution. They subvert fundamental freedom of expression rights and pose significant privacy risks.

EFF has long warned against age-gating the internet. Age verification technology itself is often inaccurate and privacy-invasive , and as more countries considering implementing ID-based checks , the risks move beyond censorship and surveillance toward excluding some people entirely. That’s why we’re working with groups in the U.S. and around the world to push back against these laws, and why we hope you join our effort.

For more information on how to fight back against dangerous age verification laws, visit our resource hub at eff.org/age

stories.summary: Premier League clubs are "concerned" about political interference in Manchester City's appeal after Prime Minister Andy Burnham's comments.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andy Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 until he became prime minister this summer

Published 8 October 2026, 10:16 BST

Some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by comments made by Andy Burnham - appearing to downplay the verdict against Manchester City - that they are now "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process, sources have told BBC Sport.

Senior club figures say they were shocked when they heard the prime minister tell the BBC he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club were found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.

They have questioned what his comments to the BBC were designed to achieve, and said it had put the Independent Football Regulator in a difficult position.

Burnham is under increasing pressure surrounding his relationship with the club's Abu Dhabi ownership during his time as mayor of Greater Manchester.

Such is the level of scrutiny that Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.

Asked to respond to the BBC's story on Thursday, Burnham said: "No I haven't downplayed the seriousness of the findings. They are findings that need to be considered with great care and seriousness and then the process that considers them needs to be fully independent.

"I said that last week and I will repeat it again. I think it's incumbent on everybody now to let the process run its course.

"I was asked a question about wider investment. I think it's important to separate the football issues from wider investment. The football issues have to be looked at fully and that is without question."

Despite clarification from Downing Street that Burnham's view is that no-one is "above the rules", his comments sparked unease among some senior Labour figures who fear his initial comments have had major cut-through with voters.

stories.body:
New ‘support and training centre’ prompts concern in region but China says it is ‘not directed at any third party’

Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new Chinese military facility in Laos , which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia.

Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows.

The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.

In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion, China opened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September.

The airport, about ⁠30 miles (50km) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway.

Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries, and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets.

The new satellite images, taken a day after the announcement and first reported by Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers.

In its announcement last week, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”.

Governments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”.

Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn of Africa .

The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway.

After years of speculation and denials , China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”.

US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos.

After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base.

“Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri.

China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while the government of Laos has not commented on the project.

The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”.

It said the base would give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes.

stories.title: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg
stories.summary: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump Here is a film for all those people who solemnly deplore social media in conversation but haven’t quite got round to deleting their accounts. Sixteen years have gone by since The Social Network , written by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher; this was the addictive, obsessive-compulsive movie about the birth of Facebook in Harvard’s macho-competitive cauldron of student sexism and nerdy self-pity, starring Jesse Eisenberg as the fast-talking, arrogant, not-necessarily-evil genius Mark Zuckerberg. Now Sorkin is back with a sequel of sorts, directing his own script – and now Zuckerberg is basically evil, but also weirdly slow talking, as if all the zinging, smart-alecky Sorkinesque dialogue energy of the first film has been siphoned away in early middle age and dispersed among the insurgents in the new cast. Sorkin’s jittery, funny, syncopated style is unmistakable, as distinctive in its way as David Mamet, although he has one joke about “spatula” being a Yiddish word that he has borrowed from Philip Roth’s Portnoy’s Complaint . It is the story of how in 2021, Zuckerberg’s Facebook empire was challenged by courageous whistleblower-employee Frances Haugen and Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, who were on a mission to tell the world how Zuckerberg, scared by falling revenue, changed the algorithm so that engagement was supercharged by rage bait and hate speech, malice and envy. Facebook, moreover, didn’t factcheck political ads, thus driving a huge, nationwide surge in extremist groups and teen bullying and becoming a major player in the Capitol riots. stories.body:
Readers respond to an article in which Larry Elliott argues that Andy Burnham must challenge neoliberal nostrums

Larry Elliott’s column on the rightwing economic myths constraining Andy Burnham’s government should be required reading before John Healey’s budget ( Rightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to Keynes, 1 October ).

I spent 20 years trading bonds, and agree that the household budget analogy bears no relation to how the UK state finances itself. Parliament votes on the spending, the Treasury instructs the Bank of England , and the Bank credits accounts in the private sector. Taxes withdraw money afterwards.

The same accounting exposes the “black hole”: every pound of government borrowing ends up as a financial asset held by households, firms and pension funds. That money hasn’t disappeared into any hole, black or otherwise.

The triple lock is debated as a question of whether Britain can afford its pensions, yet a government that issues sterling cannot run out of sterling to pay them. John Maynard Keynes and Clement Attlee understood this, and so did an unlikely ally. Asked in 2005 whether US pay-as-you-go pensions were secure, Alan Greenspan, then chair of the Federal Reserve, told Congress that there was “nothing to prevent the federal government from creating as much money as it wants and paying it to somebody”.

The same is true of sterling. The real question, he added, was whether the economy creates the real assets those pensions are used to buy. Deciding how to provide the care workers, homes and medicines is a political and moral question of the kind democracies exist to settle.

Elliott warns that Burnham risks becoming the prime minister who asked the right questions without finding the answers. Ending Treasury-Induced Decline, a report that I co-wrote, sets out the institutional reforms he needs. He could start by dropping the wrong question: “How will we pay for it?” Vince Gomez The 99% Organisation

Larry Elliott is right: Burnham’s government needs to challenge neoliberal ideas, “the nostrums of the past four decades”, like the one about the government being like a household, if it is to repair the damage done to our social services by the Tories. There are others which Elliott didn’t mention.

The Laffer curve cannot be accepted by a government when chronically underfunded public services are crumbling, and the richest 1% in the UK own 36.5% of all financial assets, with a value of £1.8tn. We must reject arguments against equalising capital gains and income tax and imposing wealth taxes – and of course increasing income tax when fiscal rules allow – which use this old and long-disproved Tory economic myth.

The same applies to the silly notion of trickle-down economics when tackling the excessive profits of banks and companies cashing in on the effects of war. That leads to the Bank of England’s inevitable blaming of wage increases for inflation, ignoring the relatively recent research in the US showing that that most price inflation comes from “ companies seeking to maintain profit margins ”. Bernie Evans Liverpool

Grateful thanks to Larry Elliott for demolishing the conditioned belief that we must not “max out the nation’s credit card”. Producing and spending is fundamentally important to the ultimate revival of the UK economy and the restoration of industrialisation. My late husband always insisted that we could afford what we needed to and I didn’t believe him. I do now. Val Bynner London

Dame Julia Hoggett says negative sentiment about the UK market has pushed companies to leave in the past

Published 8 October 2026, 00:00 BST

The UK needs to do more to back its own companies at a time when a growing number are choosing to list their shares in the US rather than at home, the boss of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) has told the BBC.

Dame Julia Hoggett said the government needed to make it "more attractive" to invest in the UK stock market, otherwise big firms would continue to look overseas for their next stage of growth.

Over the last few years, scores of big firms have left the London market , are considering a move or have been bought by private foreign investors.

The fear is this weakens the UK economy by reducing tax revenues and depressing business valuations.

'Take the handbrake off'

"If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so," Dame Julia told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast .

"We need to take the handbrake off."

The LSE's main market is made up of around 930 companies with a total market value of about £4.9 trillion.

Almost 40% are international businesses, hailing from over 80 countries.

But in the last few years, many firms have delisted or moved away from the LSE, including takeaway chain Just Eat, which joined the Amsterdam stock exchange, travel giant Tui which opted for Frankfurt, and Paddy Power-owner Flutter which now trades in New York.

'Stop throwing shade'

Meanwhile, the number of companies newly listing their shares in London has dwindled.

Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised.

It has coincided in a big rise of UK investment money flowing into US stocks in search of better returns.

"We talk as a nation about wanting growth in every postcode, but at the moment, a lot of us are funding growth in every zip code," Dame Julia said.

There was "no shortage of great companies and no shortage of capital", she added.

But negative sentiment about the UK market - which was often exaggerated - had contributed to companies leaving in the past, she said.

"We need to stop throwing shade at ourselves as a nation... it's a national habit."

Big Boss Interview: LSE's Dame Julia Hoggett

The boss of the London Stock Exchange speaks to the BBC about the attraction of the UK as a place for companies to list.

However, she said British people needed more "incentives" to invest in UK stocks.

She wants the government to scrap the 0.5% tax , external Britons pay when they purchase UK shares, pointing out there is no tax when they buy foreign stocks.

She also supports the idea of tax credits for Britons investing domestically. The UK had such a scheme until 2016.

Business lobbying group the Confederation of British Industry has called for urgent action to halt the exodus of firms from the London Stock Exchange.

It said that lighter regulation, better marketing and incentives for investors were needed to stem the outflow.

The government declined to say if stock market reform would be part of its Budget this month.

"As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals," a spokesman said.

stories.body:
Robert Ryman: The Real Thing is the American artist’s first major retrospective in the UK for over 30 years.

The show, at London’s Barbican Centre , brings 68 works together from the mid-1950s to the early 2010s. It is arranged thematically, without traditional wall text. There are no labels, even to identify the paintings . The exhibition follows Ryman’s thought that “you cannot understand a painting by explaining something. You can only understand painting by experience”.

Born in Nashville, Tennessee, Ryman initially aspired to be a musician. After two years playing the tenor saxophone in the US Army Reserve Corps, he moved to New York in 1952 to pursue a career as a jazz saxophonist. Claiming that he “never saw a painting until I came to New York” , he became intrigued after taking a job as a guard at the Museum of Modern Art. He began making his own works in an attempt to understand, through experience, how paintings are made.

The Real Thing charts Ryman’s decades-long investigation, from the first “professional” painting he made in 1955, right up to the year he died in 2019. During this time he experimented with different materials, from linen canvas to aluminium, waxed paper, rolled steel and fibreglass.

Like all paintings, Ryman’s works are material objects. Many pieces are remade in each installation. Some works, like Versions VI (1991), have elements that are stapled directly to the wall. As curator Wells Fray-Smith told me, this created unique problems during the hang. The Barbican’s walls had to be tested for “tenderness”, the ease with which they might take an ordinary staple, with some panels needing to be replaced with “tenderer” alternatives.

Dancing with light

Similar care has been taken over light. Few of the spotlights point directly at the works. Instead light is bounced from the floor, up onto the work.

In the main gallery, several large ceiling-mounted light boxes have been installed. In two of the side rooms, the Barbican’s windowed walls are similarly converted. These create the diffuse, atmospheric light that Ryman’s work demands. In the side rooms in particular the effect is subtle and rewarding, because the source is changing, natural light. The paintings seem to shift, while thin flashes of colour, breaking on the paintings’ edges, pulsate.

The fine variation of surface and light in Ryman’s paintings is lost in reproduction. The experience of visual art is temporal, like listening to music. By contrast, a photographic reproduction collapses a changing experience into a static, unchanging representation. Ryman’s works suffer badly from this effect, because his paintings rely so much on their variability of appearance through patient observation, shifting light conditions and the movement of the viewer. Don’t let the images accompanying this review guide your expectations.

One work that demonstrates this contingency of experience is Best or Worst (1996-1997). Hung above eye level in the main hall, it is composed on a matte white ground. The surface is almost covered with cadenced, horizontal, creamy-white strokes, a glossy, almost perfect white haunted by a memory of green.

These brushstrokes reflect the light, bustling as the viewer moves: the effect is joyous, like shoaling fish. As with many of his paintings, textual symbols anchor the composition: one matte, pale grey “96” in the centre, another top right, with a smaller number “7”, a typical self-reflection on the painting’s date of creation.

Ryman’s works guilelessly report the facts of their making while, simultaneously, they exceed them in the viewer’s visual experience. Some of them resemble tests that have been taken to conclusion. Others are just his signature, repeated. There is an oblique charm about how they are made, or fixed to the wall. His works are simple objects, not paintings of scenes, just paintings. He once stuck a Coke can to the wall adjacent to a painting, so he could photograph the work and retain a sense of scale. They are both objects in the world.

Ryman’s studio

The sense of the artist’s studio is present throughout the show. Although there is no textual interpretation, there is a video in a side room of the artist talking. Upstairs there is a display of archival material, including his Associated Musicians of New York Membership Card from the 1950s, paint tests from 1963 and several photographs of the artist in his studio.

Ryman’s work is singular and innovative, nevertheless, it reflects his contemporaries Sol LeWitt and Frank Stella (Stella’s early work in particular) and his germinal inspiration, Mark Rothko .

But there are the ghosts of other artists too. I was surprised when looking at the monumental centrepiece of the show, Surface Veil II (ca. 1970), to be reminded of the fleeting light of Pierre Bonnard’s large, later work .

Untitled (Background Music), (ca. 1962), in one of the upper galleries, is an energetic cluster of glyphic, textured marks on raw canvas, painted in veils of rust and ochre, largely obscured by an upper layer of white. Terminating or bending at the edge, the strokes form a frame that bounds the painting’s energy, like the walls in a music-filled room. This work made me think of the strange ink drawings made by poet Henri Michaux , in which clusters of caligraphic forms congregate the other side of meaning, an experience of language without words.

Ryman’s work is resistant to language, to reproduction, even to interpretation. It won’t perform on social media, or succumb to the relentless current of information through the attention economy. It demands all of that attention for itself.

stories.title: What’s your apocalypse skill? Finding a future-proof hobby can bring fulfilment today
stories.summary: PV productions/Shutterstock In online “prepper” communities – where people discuss ways to prepare for potential emergencies and disruptions – members often jokingly refer to their “zombie apocalypse” skills . In online “prepper” communities – where people discuss ways to prepare for potential emergencies and disruptions – members often jokingly refer to their “zombie apocalypse” skills .

These are the capabilities they would bring to catastrophic or post-apocalyptic worlds , where the demands of today’s job market suddenly matter less. Participants ask questions and exchange tips, debate ethical scenarios, and support those increasingly anxious about shortages, instability or the prospect of civil unrest.

These “apocalypse skill” musings can work to reinforce ideas that the superior value of physical strength and traditionally masculine skills will be restored by a catastrophe . But these discussions can also have the opposite effect. They can recast domestic and caring labour – the provision of food, water, comfort and support – and the work of maintenance and repair , from underpaid, low-status activities to essential skills for survival.

Hobbies can bring joy, wellbeing and focus to our busy lives, but so many of us don’t have one. If you’re ready to replace scrolling with stitching, or hustle with horticulture, The Hobby Starter Kit (a new series from Quarter Life ) will help you get going.

The typical image of a prepper puts too much emphasis on their stuff – stockpiles of food and water at home or equipment packed in emergency grab-bags – and too little on the importance preppers place on learning survival skills.

A stockpile of food simply buys you time, while a bag of survival equipment is only useful if you know what to do with it. As one prepper adage puts it: “the more you know, the less you carry.”

Practical, hands-on skills related to securing basic everyday needs are revalued for post-apocalyptic living. If familiar systems fail, it is the gardener, mechanic, home carer or nurse, not the investment banker, who become the highly sought-after member of any survival unit or “MAG” (mutual assistance group). This is one part of the appeal of being a prepper – reimagining your value in contexts other than the present.

But you don’t have to become a fully fledged prepper to take inspiration from the idea of learning practical skills. It’s an opportunity to take up a hobby that brings the satisfaction of making something yourself, getting closer to nature, or finding ways to respond to the pressures of work or eco-anxiety.

Apocalypse-proof hobbies

So what new skill could you develop in time for this hypothetical zombie apocalypse?

There is a burgeoning bushcraft and survival scene in the UK, with many providers offering one-day training courses as a taster. These tend to cover fire-starting , water purification, green woodworking and shelter-building. This could come in handy on your next camping trip, let alone during a “grid-down” scenario.

Foraging for wild food and medicinal plants is also highly valued, reflected in growing public interest in the UK . The foragers I spoke to in my ongoing research point to the meaning they find in reconnecting with natural, cyclical rhythms, despite climate-related disruption to seasonal patterns . Again, there is no shortage of courses and books to consult to begin learning how to forage safely. An important message, however, is to not rely on AI photo identification : that way you avoid poisoning your friends, as well as future-proofing your skills if the mobile network does go down.

Food growing , cooking and preservation skills don’t require an allotment or an expensive electric dehydrator. Instead, join a community garden or grow what you can in whatever small spaces are available. You can learn traditional methods of food preservation , and collect and reuse glass jars and bottles.

Then there is the much caricatured hobby of spoon-carving . Remember: this is not about the need for endless coffee spoons come the apocalypse, but about developing safe and competent knife skills for wider camp craft, such as making feathersticks for fire-lighting, or whittling a replacement tent peg.

Overlapping benefits

The advantage of all these hobbies is the multiple benefits they offer in different contexts. If the apocalypse never comes , well, you’ve still got home-grown tomatoes, homemade kimchi or a carved wooden spoon to show off to your friends.

Hobbies that get you outside and immersed in nature, in the flow of a practical activity and connected to a community can also be a valuable way of confronting the eco-anxiety many of us experience in the face of climate breakdown . Rather than succumbing to paralysing anxiety or self-protective denial , these environmental practices can foster a form of practical hope grounded in the simple value of doing something.

This dual benefit perspective is also an environmental argument. Many of these survival skills build preparedness not by stockpiling tins, but through enjoyable activities that create sociable communities, connect us to nature and develop more sustainable ways of living .

Approaching a new hobby as your “zombie apocalypse skill” is a playful way of recognising the multiple benefits of practical skills and how they might come into play in different contexts. At points in our lives when we can feel reduced to the lines on our CV, particularly in a challenging job market, this may be something to learn from preppers.

Imagining a future in which the way we are valued is transformed provides an opening to thinking about alternatives to the present , albeit from the enthusiastic embrace of worst case scenarios. But then, if you’re ready for the zombie apocalypse, you’re ready for anything – wooden spoon and wild garlic pesto in hand.

stories.title: Club Med, a Disney Cruise and an Exploding Starship: SpaceX Used Bystander Videos to Track Falling Debris
stories.summary: The post Club Med, a Disney Cruise and an Exploding Starship: SpaceX Used Bystander Videos to Track Falling Debris appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A document with two maps and four screenshots of videos. Two of the screenshots show an explosion in the sky. One of the screenshots shows an illuminated water slide.
stories.body:
A heavily redacted report obtained from the FAA by ProPublica reveals that SpaceX used videos from tourists and travelers in the Caribbean to help track falling debris after one of its Starship rockets exploded last year.

When SpaceX’s giant Starship rocket exploded over the Caribbean last year, the internet lit up with videos from airline passengers, island tourists and locals showing flaming debris shooting across the sky. Even some airline pilots recorded the fiery aftermath as planes scrambled to move out of its path .

Some of those videos of Starship’s seventh test flight — including ones taken from Disney and Royal Caribbean cruise ships and a Club Med resort — went on to play a role in the company’s efforts to count and track pieces of debris after the explosion, a report obtained by ProPublica says.

The report — obtained by ProPublica from the Federal Aviation Administration through a freedom of information request — shows video captured a fireball, then a shower of sparkling debris in the sky moments after the explosion. It includes maps pinpointing where the images were shot, which helped the company understand how debris tumbled to earth after the blast.

“At 1 minute 42 seconds, the debris cloud is observed transiting behind the cruise ship,” says the report, which SpaceX provided the FAA two weeks after the so-called mishap.

Such reports are required by federal rules in the days after a rocket failure and are supposed to describe what happened and where hazardous debris landed. The information is key for the FAA’s efforts to keep busy air traffic corridors safe at a time of rapid growth in the commercial space industry as companies like SpaceX develop and test rockets that they hope will eventually reach the moon and Mars.

During launches, the FAA preventively closes airspace. It has also been forced to clear areas quickly after test flights of massive spacecraft went wrong.

Starship flights 7 and 8 broke apart last year and scattered debris above airline traffic over the Caribbean. Before Flight 9, the FAA moved to greatly increase the size of the airspace it walled off pre-launch.

The agency defined its no-fly zones, which are closed to airplane traffic during a launch, and its so-called debris response areas, which are closed after a mishap, using information from SpaceX and modeling from Space Force, the branch of the military that deals with the nation’s space interests, to predict where debris might fall.

Nearly doubling those pre-launch no-fly zones “only makes sense if the prior margin was judged inadequate rather than just unlucky,” said Moriba Jah, a professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Texas at Austin.

Read More

Earlier this year, the FAA issued a warning that rocket launches could “significantly reduce safety” for airplanes, after ProPublica reported that 21 planes appeared to make sudden turns to exit or avoid an FAA-designated emergency no-fly zone in the minutes after the Flight 7 explosion. Such disruptions are likely to become more frequent. SpaceX is seeking to launch Starship up to 76 times a year from Cape Canaveral, Florida.

The FAA provided ProPublica the reports on Starship flights 7, 8 and 9 — all of which involved mishaps — after we requested them under the Freedom of Information Act. The FAA redacted the vast majority of all three reports, citing, among other things, exemptions in the law that protect confidential business information from disclosure. The blackouts were, in part, a reflection of SpaceX’s objections; FAA allowed the company to challenge the release of information it deemed proprietary.

The FAA refused to release information that would show SpaceX’s estimates of where debris fell during the three rocket failures. It’s unclear what the agency or the company knows about how close any airplanes came to falling debris.

“Withholding the underlying debris estimates makes it impossible for anyone outside SpaceX and FAA to check whether that pattern is improving or repeating,” Jah said. “Given a regulator already revised its own safety margins once, the public has a real interest in seeing the data behind both the old margin and the new one.”

The unredacted part of the report did not show whether the debris from the Flight 7 explosion fell where SpaceX and the FAA expected it to. But the references to Disney and Club Med guests’ video suggest SpaceX did not have a full picture of where the debris landed without them. “I would read it as evidence their own tracking did not carry cleanly through the debris cloud phase, so they used the public to fill the gap,” Jah said.

SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. The company has said that it learns from its mistakes and that each test improves Starship’s reliability. Last December, it said on X that “SpaceX is committed to responsibly using airspace during launches and reentries, prioritizing public safety to protect people on the ground, at sea, and in the air.”

The FAA did not respond to a request for comment, nor did Disney, Royal Caribbean or Club Med.

Ron Madler, a professor of aerospace engineering at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, said the videos could help SpaceX “either confirm their breakup models or possibly to improve them.”

The mishap report for Flight 8, which rained debris near the Bahamas, said before that flight’s explosive failure, SpaceX did not have the proper “test stand” that was capable of testing the rocket’s engines “for a full Starship mission.” The remainder of the page was blacked out, so it was unclear from the report whether the company had found another way to fully test the engines before launch.

Flights 7 and 8 both involved the same model. Both ended in engine-related failures.

Text in the report around the statement about the test stand was redacted. But Jah said it “means some part of the engine’s actual flight behavior was being verified for the first time in flight rather than on the ground.”

John Crassidis, an aerospace engineering professor at the University at Buffalo, said launching before having a fully capable test stand was likely “a cost-saving decision.” In building rockets, he said, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has used both the old approach of launching and then fixing any issues that arise, and the newer approach of running simulations and ground tests first to head off problems.

“Doing too much of the old school can lead to too many mishaps and cost overruns,” he said. “Doing too much of the new school leads to long times to get things done and a reduction in flexibility.”

stories.title: American Academy of Pediatrics Renews Call for Ban on Raw Milk
stories.summary: The post American Academy of Pediatrics Renews Call for Ban on Raw Milk appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Citing the growing popularity of unpasteurized milk and the damage it can do to children, the nation’s largest professional group of pediatricians is seeking a nationwide ban on the sale and distribution of raw dairy products.

The nation’s largest professional group of pediatricians has renewed its call for a nationwide ban on the sale and distribution of unpasteurized milk and other raw dairy products, according to a policy statement it published earlier this week.

The revised guidance from the American Academy of Pediatrics warns of the serious health risks from consuming raw dairy products, particularly for children, as well as pregnant and immunocompromised people.

“More and more people are discussing this as a potentially healthful thing to do, when in fact it’s a highly risky thing to do,” said the academy’s president, Dr. Andrew Racine. “So our responsibility, as the leading voice of pediatric healthcare in the United States that’s dedicated to the health and well-being of children, is to make sure that the accurate, evidence-based information is out there.”

The revised statement follows ProPublica reporting that dived deep into the causes and severe consequences of America’s current fascination with raw milk, which has not been heated to kill off harmful bacteria. Once limited to the fringes of health-food culture, unpasteurized milk has morphed into a widespread movement rooted in wellness trends and institutional distrust. Today, more than 10 million Americans drink it .

Most scientists and health experts agree that raw milk has no significant, proven nutritional benefits over its pasteurized counterpart and that it cannot treat or cure any disease. It also subjects its consumers to over 100 times the risk of foodborne illness, which can be especially dangerous for young children. Before milk pasteurization was widely adopted a century ago, thousands of children died each year from diseases linked to contaminated dairy.

As it has grown in popularity in recent years, raw dairy products have contributed to numerous outbreaks of pathogenic diseases, such as salmonella and E. coli . Over the past two years, nine states have experienced outbreaks that regulators have linked to raw dairy. Just last month, federal regulators linked an E. coli outbreak to unpasteurized cheese . Thirteen people fell ill, more than half of whom were young children.

As illnesses have surged, high-level lawmakers and government officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., have championed the industry instead of curbing it. In his federal role, Kennedy said he was “ advocating ” for raw milk and celebrated the release of a report to Make America Healthy Again with a toast of raw-milk shooters in the White House. The health department did not respond to ProPublica’s questions about the new professional guidance or the pediatric group’s call for a ban on raw milk sales.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro, a Connecticut Democrat who chairs the Congressional Food Safety Caucus, told ProPublica that she is taking the guidance of the academy “very seriously.”

“They see firsthand what these illnesses can do to children,” she said in an emailed statement. “Right now, Secretary of Health and Human Services RFK Jr. cannot even bring himself to tell parents not to give it to their kids.”

DeLauro said she was “supportive of any policy that reduces risk of exposure to harmful foods,” including putting warning labels on raw-milk products and maintaining adequate funding for outbreak prevention and tracking.

Federal law restricts the sale of raw milk across state lines, but states can decide how it can be sold within their boundaries. In recent years, proponents have fought to increase access to raw milk within states, often opposing efforts to limit its sales. People can legally purchase raw milk in all but a handful of states, either directly from a store or from a farmer, or even as “pet food.”

Last week, ProPublica detailed the case of two girls severely sickened last year after consuming raw goat milk from an unregulated farm in southern California. The state, which is teeming with black-market dairies, did little to punish the farmer who sold the families the milk. It allowed her to provide her own sample for testing, weeks after the outbreak began, and did not independently sample her grounds for traces of the pathogen, as state investigators have done in other cases. (The farmer told ProPublica that her milk, which tested negative for pathogens, did not cause the outbreak and claimed the families had knowingly bought milk that was not for human consumption, which they deny.)

The mother of one of the girls, a toddler who nearly died, had read about the purported benefits of unpasteurized milk on a site for the Raw Milk Institute, a nonprofit founded by Mark McAfee, one of the nation’s most prolific sellers. In a profile of the California farmer , ProPublica chronicled how social media influencers have amplified his claims and helped him build what is now a $30 million-a-year business even as regulators have linked it to more than a dozen recalls and outbreaks that have sickened hundreds. (McAfee previously defended the claims made on the institute’s website and maintained to ProPublica that raw milk still has therapeutic benefits.)

Members of the academy said they read and circulated ProPublica’s reporting as they drafted their statement.

“This product is being marketed to families as being beneficial for their kids,” said Dr. Adam Ratner, a pediatric infectious disease doctor in New York City and one of the lead authors of the academy’s revised statement. “They don’t see the risks, and unwittingly they end up making a decision that is much more dangerous.”

The academy first published a policy statement on raw milk in 2014, endorsing a nationwide ban on its sale and encouraging its members to reach out to state representatives to advocate for such a restriction. The statement published this week reaffirms this appeal with recent epidemiological evidence. In addition, it cites a growing concern of highly pathogenic avian influenza, which has been shown to contaminate unpasteurized milk .

Racine, the academy’s president, told ProPublica that the policy was also updated on account of “the rise in the discussion about the alleged benefits of raw milk and the fact that more people are experimenting with using it.”

“Prevention really is the best single way to keep children healthy and safe, and this is a preventive move,” he said. “The more that we can disseminate this information to a greater number of people, the healthier we’re going to be able to keep the children of this country.”

stories.title: The U.S. Public Is Losing Its Say on Environmental Policy
stories.summary: Federal agencies have long been required to seek public comment when writing new regulations or approving large projects, from highways to data centers. The Trump administration is systematically undercutting that process, stifling public input while skirting federal laws. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A hearing room in the headquarters of the Environmental Protection Agency in Washington, D.C. Carol M. Highsmith / Buyenlarge / Getty Images

OPINION

Federal agencies have long been required to seek public comment when writing new regulations or approving large projects, from highways to data centers. The Trump administration is systematically undercutting that process, stifling public input while skirting federal laws.

By Jody Freeman • October 8, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Public participation is a hallmark of environmental regulation, embedded in every major environmental statute enacted over the past half-century. Yet the Trump administration has systematically sought to curtail public input into the government’s environmental decision-making by shirking decades of precedent and making strained interpretations of longstanding federal law. Looked at collectively, the pattern of public disenfranchisement is unmistakable.

There are good reasons to speed up the process of writing regulations and issuing permits, but truncating public input has serious costs. It can result in flawed policy that is harder to implement, full of avoidable error, and more vulnerable to being struck down by courts. Input from industry, public interest groups, academics, states, and other agencies gives regulators critical feedback on the potential impact of their proposed rules, helping them to anticipate and avoid unforeseen problems. Stakeholders possess information, experience, and expertise the government lacks, and they can suggest alternatives to make rules more effective or less costly. By testing agency assumptions and pushing officials to explain their rationale, public comments perform a crucial vetting function. The process also helps to make government more accountable by alerting Congress to potential pitfalls and building a record in the event of judicial review.

In 2025, the administration began stifling public input on the rigorous environmental reviews required by the 1969 National Environmental Policy Act. Under this law, federal agencies must evaluate and disclose the foreseeable environmental impacts of the major projects they build, fund, or approve, from highways to dams to data centers. The point of NEPA disclosure is to avoid unnecessary harm by having agencies look before they leap.

Finalizing rules quickly has appeal, but it could result in rules that are less sound and more vulnerable to legal challenge.

The process can delay projects, but it can also improve them substantially. Studies show that public-comment requirements and stakeholder engagement have repeatedly identified environmental risks that proposing agencies had missed. Often, significant harms can be reduced by taking sensible steps, like rerouting roads around sensitive areas, as was done with Utah’s Legacy Parkway, which was redesigned to largely avoid the Great Salt Lake wetlands. In another example, the Energy Department amended its permitting plan for the Los Alamos National Laboratory to include a comprehensive wildfire-mitigation program after commenters focused attention on the risks of wildfire. These steps significantly reduced impacts when a fire later burned the region.

For this process to work, however, the government must share its draft impact statements with the public, which past Republican and Democratic administrations have done. The Trump administration lifted that obligation, though, and agencies including Interior, Agriculture, Energy, and Transportation announced last year that they will no longer share drafts, making informed public comment practically impossible. Several agencies have also jettisoned the requirement to analyze proposed projects’ indirect and cumulative impacts, like climate change. The agencies made these changes without taking comment first, thus narrowing public involvement without public involvement.

A 2011 fire near the Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico. Public commenters drew attention to the risk of wildfires when the lab was undergoing environmental review. Jae C. Hong / Associated Press

The Trump administration’s efforts to suppress public input are part of a larger backlash in which critics on both the right and left claim that procedural red tape strangles worthy projects. Some of this criticism is fair, but it can be overdrawn. Infrastructure projects falter for many reasons , including high costs, supply chain problems, and opposition from rival developers. Environmental reviews may be part of the problem, but project timelines would be shorter if agencies followed NEPA rules more carefully from a project’s inception. Congress already limited the scope and length of environmental reviews in 2023, and while more steps are needed to streamline federal permitting, that can be done without jettisoning valuable public consultation.

The permitting reform legislation proposed in the Senate in September would, among other things, drastically limit legal remedies when agencies violate NEPA, barring courts from delaying projects even when the agencies make blatant errors in environmental reviews. If projects proceed no matter what, there is little incentive to engage the public. The changes might speed up projects, but they will also result in many avoidable and unnecessary harms.

The administration has stymied public participation by declaring emergencies and citing national security, among other tactics.

In addition to thwarting comments on new projects, the administration is also marginalizing comments on new regulations. The president has directed agencies to issue rules without taking input first, citing the “good cause” exception to the requirement in the Administrative Procedure Act that agencies publish their proposed rules in the Federal Register, triggering a 30- or 60-day comment period. Decades of legal precedent holds that agencies may finalize rules before taking comment only in exceptional cases where they can justify the urgency — for example, where the rule is necessary to foil terrorism, respond to a public health emergency, or prevent investors from gaming the market in anticipation of a regulatory change.

Finalizing rules more quickly has obvious appeal — the current system is slow and cumbersome and blocks both Republican and Democratic administrations from getting things done. But shunting public input to the end of the process will not solve that problem if rules are less sound, prone to error, and more vulnerable to legal challenge as a result.

In another example of limiting public participation, the EPA is proposing to drop a longstanding federal requirement that state and local air agencies allow the public to comment on air pollution permits for new “minor” sources that emit pollution below a certain threshold. This classification could include data centers that divide up their power generation units to make each source appear smaller. These permits are highly controversial because data centers powered by gas or diesel generators emit substantial air pollution. But the rule change could allow these permits to be fast-tracked without any opportunity for the public to weigh in.

Gas turbines at an xAI data center in Memphis, Tennessee. The Trump administration is trying to dismiss a citizen suit against the data center. Brandon Dill for The Washington Post via Getty Images

Besides undercutting notice and comment, the administration has stymied public participation in a broad range of environmental decisions by declaring emergencies and citing national security, among other tactics. For example, in March, the Interior Department invoked a never-before-used national security exemption to relieve the oil and natural gas industry of Endangered Species Act requirements in the Gulf of Mexico on the rationale that court rulings enforcing the law might hamper energy production, which the administration linked to national security. In 2025, President Trump granted two-year exemptions from Clean Air Act hazardous air pollution standards to coal plants, coke ovens, and chemical manufacturers, invoking for the first time a national security-based provision in the Clean Air Act.

In another gambit in June, the EPA found a creative way to revoke three waivers that allowed California to set its own clean car standards: by relabeling them as rules and submitting them to Congress for fast-track “disapproval” under the Congressional Review Act. Both the Government Accountability Office and the Senate Parliamentarian objected to this maneuver but were ignored. Normally, waiver rescissions would require public notice and comment. (A district court has blocked EPA from relabeling a second batch of waivers.)

Separately, the administration is trying to frustrate the citizen suit provisions that Congress included in virtually every major environmental law passed in the 1970s and 1980s. Under these provisions, individuals or groups may file a lawsuit against regulated entities for statutory or regulatory violations (unless the federal government is “diligently prosecuting” the same violations). Citizen suits may also be brought against federal agencies for failing to perform congressionally mandated duties, like setting pollution standards by certain deadlines. This summer, in response to a citizen suit by a coalition of states and nonprofit groups, a federal court held that the EPA had failed to identify areas with unhealthy levels of soot pollution — a first step toward applying stricter control measures — by the legal deadline and ordered it to do so by early next year. (The administration is appealing.)

Research shows that when people participate in decisions that affect them, they are more likely to view those decisions as legitimate.

While it’s true that private enforcement actions can be inconvenient for an administration, there is no doubt that citizen suits have profoundly improved conditions for communities affected by harmful pollution. Both Republican and Democratic administrations have sometimes objected to these suits, but no administration has sought to eliminate them.

Until this summer, that is, when the Trump administration intervened in a citizen suit against xAI for violating the Clean Air Act when generating power for its data centers. The administration claims that the president may demand that a court dismiss a citizen suit for any reason, whether the administration is diligently prosecuting violations or not.

Public participation does take time, but it is valuable to governance. It gives regulated industries, professional associations, public interest groups, experts, other agencies, states, and individuals a chance to be heard. It also helps to build trust in government. As quaint as that claim may sound, it is backed up by evidence. Research shows that when people participate in decisions that affect them, they are more likely to view those decisions as legitimate, even when they don’t go their way. Having a voice matters. There are good reasons to reform our regulatory and permitting system, but not by dispensing with public participation.
